source.version: Working paper, The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, dated January 27, 2024 (p. 1). The document shows no SSRN number; the search record gives DOI 10.2139/ssrn.4708466.
source.title_on_document: Prompting Diverse Ideas: Increasing AI Idea Variance

supplement.where: Appendices A to F at the end of this PDF (pp. 18-38). The paper refers to no separate online supplement and gives no data or code URL.
supplement.holds: Appendix D (pp. 20-36) lists each strategy's prompt, cosine similarity, and pool size, including 'Student Ideas 0.243 10x100' and a programmatic 'Lowest Cosine Add' pool (0.144, 1x100) that Table 2 omits. Appendix F (pp. 37-38) gives the population equation and code for the unique-ideas estimate. No standard errors appear in the main text or the appendices.

paper_design_summary: The authors prompt GPT-4 with 35 prompting strategies (base prompt, personas, creativity articles, emotional appeals, hybrid brainstorming, similarity information, Chain-of-Thought) to generate pools of new-product ideas for US college students priced under about USD 50, mostly 10 sessions of 100 ideas per strategy. They score each pool's diversity as the mean pairwise cosine similarity of Google Universal Sentence Encoder embeddings and compare the pools with each other, with two GPT-4 pools labeled 'Girota et al.', and with an existing pool of Wharton MBA student ideas reused from Girotra et al. (2023). A separate analysis generates about 1,200 ideas per session with the base and Chain-of-Thought prompts to estimate the number of unique ideas and the speed of exhaustion; no person receives AI help and no participants are recruited.

studies.label: GPT-4 idea pools versus a pool of Wharton MBA student ideas (within-pool cosine similarity, Table 2)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was assigned to people. The authors generate GPT-4 idea pools under different prompts and compare them with an existing pool of student ideas reused from Girotra et al. (2023).
assignment.quote: As a baseline for comparison, we use a pool consisting of 100 randomly chosen ideas generated by Wharton MBA students. This is the same pool of ideas used as in Girotra et al 2023.
assignment.locator: p. 5, section 'Prompting Strategies for Innovation and Brainstorming'

arms.name: Group of Students
arms.description: Existing pool of Wharton MBA student ideas, aggregated from multiple students working individually and reused from Girotra et al. (2023) (p. 5). Size: 100 randomly chosen ideas per p. 5, but Appendix D (p. 20) lists 'Student Ideas' as 10x100; the paper does not reconcile the two. Cosine similarity 0.243 (Table 2, p. 11).

arms.name: GPT-4 Base Prompt
arms.description: GPT-4 (gpt4-0314, temperature 0.7, top P 1.0) with the base prompt; 10x100 ideas over 10 sessions (p. 5; p. 8; Appendix D, p. 24). Cosine similarity 0.377 (Table 2, p. 11).

arms.name: GPT-4 Chain of Thought (gpt4-1106-preview)
arms.description: Three-step prompt: list 100 short titles, make them bolder and more different, then write 40-80-word descriptions; run on gpt4-1106-preview because of the context limits of gpt-4-0314; 10x100 ideas (p. 6; p. 12; Appendix A, p. 18; Appendix D, p. 20). Cosine similarity 0.255 (Table 2, p. 11).

arms.name: Other GPT-4 prompting strategies
arms.description: The remaining GPT-4 rows of Table 2 (persona and modifier prompts such as Steve Jobs, Sam Altman, Elon Musk, entrepreneur, creative entrepreneur, creative AI, boring person, and think bold; tipping, emotional appeals, threats, and politeness; HBR and Stanford design-thinking articles; previous top ideas; cosine information; hybrid brainstorming, which simulates 40 GPT-4 'participants') plus two GPT-4 pools labeled 'Girota et al. Baseline GPT-4' and 'Girota et al. Seeded GPT-4'. Most are 10x100; Hybrid Brainstorming and the two Girota et al. pools are 1x100 (Appendix D, pp. 30, 34). Cosine similarity 0.348 to 0.432 (Table 2, p. 11).

participants.exclusions: No new participants were recruited. Exclusions for the reused student-idea pool are not stated (pp. 5-6, Prompting Strategies for Innovation and Brainstorming).
participants.who: No participants are recruited. The human comparison is an existing pool of ideas by Wharton MBA students, reused from Girotra et al. (2023) and aggregated from multiple students; the paper does not say how many students contributed.
participants.quote: It is important to note that students were not tasked with generating 100 ideas at once, but instead the pool is an aggregation of ideas from multiple students.
participants.locator: p. 5, section 'Prompting Strategies for Innovation and Brainstorming'

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4: gpt4-0314 (temperature 0.7, top P 1.0) unless otherwise stated; gpt4-1106-preview for Chain-of-Thought
ai_tool.how_used: The researchers prompt GPT-4 to generate idea pools directly; no human participant is assigned AI assistance. The two Girota et al. pools are labeled as coming from that earlier work (pp. 5-6; p. 11, Table 2).

task.description: Generate ideas for a new physical consumer product for college students in the United States, retail price under about USD 50, each idea a named paragraph of 40-80 words (base prompt, p. 12).

outcomes.name: Mean within-pool cosine similarity of ideas (higher = more similar = less diverse)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity of Google Universal Sentence Encoder embeddings between all ideas in a pool, computed per pool and averaged over the pools of a strategy (p. 9). Table 2 (p. 11) prints one number per strategy; Figure 2 (p. 10) shows density plots for nine selected strategies. Pools: 10x100 ideas for most strategies; 1x100 for Hybrid Brainstorming and the two Girota et al. pools (Appendix D, pp. 30, 34); the student pool is 100 ideas per p. 5 but 10x100 per Appendix D (p. 20). Appendix A (p. 18) mentions robustness runs with gpt4-0314 on pools of 30 ideas, with no results printed.

contrasts.reported: Cosine similarity: Base Prompt 0.377 vs Group of Students 0.243 (Table 2). These are pool-level similarity summaries. Direction coded for diversity: higher similarity means a less diverse pool. No pair-specific p-value, SE, CI, test statistic, or standardized effect is printed. The general bootstrap/permutation statement on p. 9 reports p-values below 0.01 without identifying this contrast; it is recorded in diversity_detail.uncertainty. Figure 2 legend: Group of Students (0.243), Base (0.377).
contrasts.locator: p. 11, Table 2; p. 9, Results; p. 10, Figure 2

contrasts.reported: Cosine similarity: Chain Of Thought (gpt4-1106-preview) 0.255 vs Group of Students 0.243 (Table 2). These are pool-level similarity summaries. Direction coded for diversity: the CoT pool is slightly less diverse; the paper calls CoT "a close second" (p. 9). No pair-specific p-value, SE, CI, test statistic, or standardized effect is printed. The general bootstrap/permutation statement on p. 9 does not identify this contrast. Figure 2 legend: Chain of Thought (0.255).
contrasts.locator: p. 11, Table 2; p. 3, main findings; p. 9, Results; p. 10, Figure 2

diversity_detail.metric: Mean pairwise cosine similarity among the ideas within a pool (higher = less diverse)
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of ideas within each pool (within-pool comparison), averaged over the pools of each strategy: 10 pools of 100 ideas for most GPT-4 strategies (each prompt run 'at least 10 times', p. 9); one pool of 100 for Hybrid Brainstorming and the two Girota et al. pools (Appendix D). The student pool is 100 ideas per p. 5 but 10x100 per Appendix D (p. 20).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Bootstrapping and permutation testing of differences between pools, 'p-values below 0.01' (p. 9), and 'The differences between pools of 1000 ideas become significant at ~0.01' (p. 9). The paper does not state the resampling unit; it ties significance to 'the large number of ideas'. No standard errors, intervals, or pair-specific tests are printed.
diversity_detail.notes: Figure 2 legend (p. 10) prints Creative Entrepreneur (0.347) and Brainstorming (0.396), while Table 2 (p. 11) prints Creative Entrepreneur 0.348 and Hybrid Brainstorming 0.393. Appendix D (p. 20) also lists a programmatic 'Lowest Cosine Add' pool at 0.144 (1x100) that Table 2 omits. The limitations (p. 15) say the aggregated 'team human' pool is likely more diverse than any individual or brainstorming team could produce.

studies.label: GPT-4 prompt-versus-prompt comparisons, unique-ideas and exhaustion analysis, and between-pool overlap (model only)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Prompting strategy for GPT-4 idea generation; no people take part.

assignment.locator: p. 5, section 'Prompting Strategies for Innovation and Brainstorming'

participants.exclusions: No participants. Chain-of-Thought runs in which the model skipped the second step were removed, 'around ~15% of all runs' (p. 12, Exhaustion section); the paper does not say whether this also applies to the Table 2 Chain-of-Thought pools.
participants.who: No human participants; GPT-4 output only. Hybrid brainstorming simulates 40 GPT-4 'participants', not people (p. 5).
participants.quote: For both strategies, we generate around 1200 ideas while keeping all previous ideas in the context window. Each prompt is run 5 times and the results are averaged.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4: gpt4-0314 for the prompt comparisons; gpt4-1106-preview for Chain-of-Thought and the exhaustion analysis
ai_tool.how_used: GPT-4 generates ideas under different prompts. The exhaustion analysis generates about 1,200 ideas per session in 30-idea increments while keeping all previous ideas in context, 5 runs per prompt (p. 9).

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: Girotra, Meincke, Terwiesch, and Ulrich (2023), 'Ideas are dimes a dozen: Large language models for idea generation in innovation' (SSRN 4526071; screened here as c007): the student idea pool is the same pool. Table 2 also includes two GPT-4 pools labeled 'Girota et al. Baseline GPT-4' and 'Girota et al. Seeded GPT-4'. Meincke and Terwiesch are authors of both papers (p. 1; p. 16).
sample_overlap.quote: As a baseline for comparison, we use a pool consisting of 100 randomly chosen ideas generated by Wharton MBA students. This is the same pool of ideas used as in Girotra et al 2023.

company_involvement.description: None stated. The authors list only the Wharton School (p. 1, footnote 1). The paper names GPT-4 model versions (gpt4-0314, gpt4-1106-preview) but does not name OpenAI or an API, and it prints no funding statement or acknowledgments.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1, footnote 1; p. 8, Technical set-up; p. 18, Appendix A

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is not met: GPT-4 generates the AI idea pools directly, and the human comparison reuses student ideas from Girotra et al. (2023); no people are randomly assigned to AI assistance (pp. 5-6, Prompting Strategies for Innovation and Brainstorming). Criterion 2 is unclear for S1: the paper reports ideas, not the number of distinct students whose output is analyzed. Page 5 says 100 randomly chosen student ideas, whereas Appendix D lists Student Ideas as 10x100 (p. 20); neither establishes at least 50 people. Criterion 3 is met for S1: diversity is computed on the idea text, including the human-produced student pool, using Universal Sentence Encoder embeddings and average within-pool cosine similarity (p. 9, Technical set-up; p. 11, Table 2). S1 is ai_vs_human context, and S2 is model-only. Core eligibility is definitively no because criterion 1 fails, regardless of the unresolved student count.

one_line_finding: GPT-4 idea pools have higher within-pool cosine similarity, so less diversity, than a pool of Wharton MBA student ideas (0.377 for the base prompt and 0.255 for Chain-of-Thought versus 0.243 for students; 0.255 to 0.432 across GPT-4 pools; Table 2, p. 11; p. 3), and Chain-of-Thought raises the estimated number of unique ideas from about 3,700 to about 4,700 (p. 13).
open_questions: Student-pool sampling and aggregation remain unresolved: p. 5 reports 100 randomly chosen ideas, while Appendix D (p. 20) lists Student Ideas as 10x100. Author clarification is needed to establish which pools were analyzed and how the reported 0.243 was aggregated.

The number of distinct Wharton MBA students contributing to the human idea pool analyzed in c014 is not stated (pp. 5-6). A verified count of contributors to this specific analyzed pool is needed for criterion 2; the number of ideas cannot substitute for people.
notes: Reconciled from forms A and B. Model-only results (S2), recorded here rather than as outcomes: opportunity space about 3700 ideas for the base prompt (13.8% repetitive) vs about 4700 for Chain-of-Thought (11.7%), from a 0.8 cosine threshold and the Kornish and Ulrich mark-recapture equation (p. 8; p. 13; Appendix F, pp. 37-38); in the exhaustion analysis the Chain-of-Thought advantage in cosine similarity persists to about 750 ideas and is strongest between 100 and 500 ideas (p. 12; Figure 3, p. 13); between-pool overlap among the first 50 ideas of each pool is small (p. 13; Figure 4, p. 14). Prompt contrasts in Table 2 include Steve Jobs 0.368 vs base 0.377 and the HBR article 0.387 (p. 3; p. 11). No data or code URL is given; Appendix F prints code for the population estimate. S2 population is left empty because no people take part. Both screeners omitted source.supplement; the reconciler filled it from the PDF. Final review: no c014 challenge files were present. The complete markdown, including Appendices A-F, was read; recorded result values were checked against the PDF text and recovered tables, and Figure 2 was checked visually. Eligibility criteria are assessed separately: the reused human-output score meets criterion 3, while the unreported number of contributing students leaves criterion 2 unclear; no random assignment to AI means core remains no. The context-class question is settled by codebook sections 3-4 and the human-versus-model comparison in H1 and Table 2: retain S1 as ai_vs_human context. Reuse of a human idea pool does not establish a randomized AI-assistance experiment. The two contrast-level statistics_available fields are set to none because Table 2 supplies similarity summaries without any of the listed pair-specific inferential statistics or complete mean/SD/n summaries; the general p-values below 0.01 remain in diversity_detail.uncertainty. Student country is not inferred from the authors' affiliation. The reconciliation object is preserved as the earlier audit record; final eligibility and contrast fields supersede its corresponding earlier judgments. The final n_corrected, n_rejected, and n_open fields count challenge resolutions only.

differences.a: Two studies: S1 ai_vs_human (GPT-4 pools vs the student pool, Table 2) and S2 model_only (35-prompt comparison and exhaustion analysis); S2 population 'students'.
differences.b: One study, S1 ai_vs_human, labeled to cover cosine similarity, unique ideas, and exhaustion; open question notes that it could be read as model_only.
differences.resolved: Two studies, as in A. S1 ai_vs_human: the cosine-similarity comparison of GPT-4 pools with the student pool (H1, Table 2). S2 model_only: prompt-versus-prompt comparisons, the unique-ideas and exhaustion analysis (separate sessions of about 1,200 ideas, base vs Chain-of-Thought), and between-pool overlap. Unique ideas and exhaustion are computed only for GPT-4 prompts, so B's S1 label does not fit the human comparison. S2 population set to empty, since no people take part.

open_items.item: Original open question about the student-pool size and the unresolved reconciliation difference studies[S1].arms[Group of Students] pool size: p. 5 says 100 randomly chosen ideas, while Appendix D, p. 20, says Student Ideas 0.243 10x100. Authors must clarify the analyzed pools and aggregation behind 0.243. This concerns output sampling, not a count of people, and does not itself decide an eligibility criterion.

The same unresolved reconciliation difference also asks how many students contributed. The number of distinct people represented in the analyzed student pool is not reported (pp. 5-6). An author-confirmed contributor count for this specific pool would settle criterion 2. This could change criterion 2 but cannot overcome the confirmed failure of criterion 1.

Original open question about ai_vs_human context versus model-only exclusion is resolved: H1 (p. 5) and Table 2 (p. 11) explicitly compare GPT-4 and student idea pools. Codebook sections 3-4 place S1 in ai_vs_human context; the separate model-only S2 analyses remain excluded from the core. No additional source is needed.
